strengths: Simple, training-free, plug-and-play intervention (entropy-gated selective CFG with KV-cache-reused negative prompting) that is genuinely low-overhead in design and orthogonal to test-time scaling approaches

Broad empirical coverage: three model sizes, base and reasoning modes, and eight benchmarks spanning general, coding, and STEM domains, with a clear efficiency-vs-usage tradeoff reported via 'CFG Usage' columns

Useful diagnostic analyses: the entropy-localization observation (Fig. 1), the analysis of which tokens vanilla CFG can actually modify (Fig. 5) provides a principled justification for entropy-based gating, and ablations over threshold τ, guidance strength ω, and negative-prompt choice
The lightweight negative-prompt construction via KV-cache reuse is a practical contribution that avoids the double-cache cost of vanilla LLM-CFG
weaknesses: Statistical rigor of gains is insufficient: most main results (Table 2) use greedy decoding with no variance or significance testing, and several benchmarks are tiny (AIME2024 has 30 problems; GPQA-Diamond ~198), so headline claims like +5% on AIME may be within noise; the average improvement is small (e.g., +0.78 for Qwen3-32B-Reasoning, and several MTI settings perform worse than direct inference)

Hyperparameter sensitivity is not resolved: accuracy is non-monotonic in τ, the best τ differs per model (1.5 for 8B-Base vs 1.0 for 8B-Reasoning), and some high-τ settings underperform the baseline (e.g., 74.72 vs 75.38 for Qwen3-32B-Reasoning at τ=2.0), leaving no principled rule for choosing τ in practice

The central efficiency claim ('highly efficient', 'negligible overhead') is never quantified: no wall-clock latency, FLOPs, or memory measurements are reported for the per-intervention 3-token forward pass; also, all experiments use only the Qwen3 family, so cross-family generalization is untested

Missing comparisons to closely related decoding-time methods that also use entropy or contrastive guidance (e.g., contrastive decoding/search variants), and no compute-matched comparison against baselines like self-consistency

The motivation in Fig. 1 is largely correlational—incorrect answers meandering and thus having higher entropy is somewhat expected—and the inset counts are unnormalized; minor presentation issues include a missing minus sign in Eq. 2 and qualitative-only word-cloud analysis

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is stated; the appendix lists only OpenCompass config file names, without exact prompt templates, negative-prompt injection mechanics, or sampling configurations for the greedy vs. stochastic experiments

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the core idea—restricting CFG-style intervention to the small fraction of high-entropy tokens and reusing the conditional KV cache instead of maintaining a second unconditional cache—is simple, practical, and plausibly useful.

The evaluation is broad in scope: three model sizes of the Qwen3 family, both Base and Reasoning variants, and eight benchmarks spanning general, coding, and math/science tasks, with hyperparameter ablations over the entropy threshold, guidance strength, and negative prompt.

The diagnostic analysis (Fig. 1, Fig. 5) linking high-entropy tokens to reasoning failures and to tokens actually changed by CFG is a reasonable empirical observation, and the implementation details (thresholds, omega, negative prompt, OpenCompass configs, sampling protocol for AIME2024) are reported at a level that partially supports reproduction.
The method is training-free and adds little overhead, which makes it easy for practitioners to try, and the efficiency motivation (avoiding dual KV caches of vanilla LLM-CFG) is well articulated.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim—that gains come from CFG steering away from a well-constructed 'unconditional/error space'—is not adequately supported. The ablation shows 'OUTPUT TRUE' also improves over direct inference (59.09 vs 57.07), which suggests that simply appending arbitrary tokens at high-entropy positions may perturb decoding and inject diversity, regardless of the prompt's 'negative' semantics. A critical control experiment with a neutral/semantically unrelated string (e.g., 'HELLO WORLD') or random token injection is missing, and without it the CFG framing may be post-hoc rationalization of a generic perturbation effect.

Gains are small and inconsistent. The headline average improvement is only +1.35 points, and across Table 2 several settings actually degrade performance relative to direct inference (e.g., Qwen3-8B-Reasoning at tau=0.1: 69.32 vs 70.39; Qwen3-32B-Reasoning at tau=0.1: 74.67 vs 75.38; WinoGrande drops of 3-4 points are common). The paper selectively highlights best-case configurations without reporting variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, so it is unclear the improvements are robust rather than noise.

Evaluation is limited to a single model family (Qwen3). For a decoding-time method whose value rests on generality, at least one additional family (Llama, Mistral, etc.) would be needed to support the claim that the effect generalizes beyond a specific architecture.

AIME2024 has only 30 problems; even eight sampled runs yield high-variance estimates, and the main tables use greedy decoding where single-run differences of 1-2 points on small benchmarks can easily be noise. No statistical testing is provided anywhere.

The contribution is incremental relative to existing work. Entropy-based localization of critical reasoning tokens is well established (Wang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2025, all cited by the authors), and CFG for LLMs is from Sanchez et al. (2023). The novelty reduces to combining these two ideas plus a KV-cache reuse trick for the negative-prompt branch, which the paper does not position sharply enough against these closely related methods experimentally (no head-to-head with e.g. contrastive decoding or high-entropy-token RL/prioritization baselines at matched compute).

The theoretical framing is muddled: the paper argues LLMs 'lack a well-defined unconditional space' yet claims an ad-hoc two-token appended phrase yields a 'better-calibrated approximation' to it, without formal or empirical justification of what this branch actually computes. Equation (1) as written is also ambiguous about the roles of the conditional and negative contexts.

Some claims are internally inconsistent or weakly supported: the 'principled justification' for entropy-based selection rests on a single correlational histogram (Fig. 5); the word-cloud analysis (Fig. 4) is qualitative and anecdotal; and the case study (Fig. 6) is a single cherry-picked example.
No code release is mentioned, and the KV-cache-reuse implementation is nontrivial in inference engines like vLLM, limiting reproducibility of the exact efficiency claims.

The efficiency benefit is understated analytically: the paper never reports wall-clock latency or memory overhead numbers, despite efficiency being a headline motivation ('almost no extra test-time computation' is asserted, not measured).

strengths: The paper identifies a simple and practically relevant phenomenon—reasoning uncertainty is concentrated in a small subset of high-entropy tokens—and builds a clean, training-free decoding intervention (MTI) around it.

The evaluation is broad: six Qwen3 variants (8B/14B/32B, Base/Reasoning) across eight benchmarks spanning general knowledge, math/science, and coding, plus AIME2024 under stochastic sampling with multiple seeds.

The ablation studies (entropy threshold, guidance strength ω, negative-prompt choice) are reasonably thorough, and Fig. 5 provides a principled empirical justification for skipping CFG at low-entropy positions.

The efficiency motivation is well taken: avoiding a second KV cache and applying CFG to only ~1–10% of tokens makes the method attractive relative to vanilla LLM-CFG, which the paper shows can hurt performance.
The method is training-free and plug-and-play, which increases practical impact and ease of adoption; the OpenCompass setup details in the appendix aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Average gains are small (e.g., +1.35% on Qwen3-8B-Base) and no statistical significance testing or variance estimates are reported for the deterministic (greedy) benchmark results; on benchmarks like WinoGrande and MMLU-Pro with hundreds to thousands of items, sub-1-point differences may be within noise.

Results in Table 1 fluctuate non-monotonically and substantially with the threshold τ (e.g., Qwen3-14B: 79.58, 80.83, 81.67, 78.33, 80.00 on AIME2024), suggesting sensitivity to noise; the best configuration appears to be selected per model on the test benchmarks (bold 'Avg' per row), which risks overfitting hyperparameters (τ, ω) to evaluation data.

The central mechanistic claim—that appending 'OUTPUT ERROR' to the reused KV cache yields a 'better approximation to the unconditional space'—is asserted rather than demonstrated. No analysis shows what distribution this modified context actually induces or why it behaves like a negative/unconditional branch; the interpretation is plausible but under-supported.

The motivating correlation in Fig. 1 (incorrect answers have higher entropy) is expected post-hoc behavior and does not by itself establish that stabilizing high-entropy tokens will improve correctness; the causal link is only supported indirectly through the results.

Missing comparisons to relevant baselines: other decoding-time interventions such as contrastive decoding variants, entropy-triggered re-sampling at uncertain positions, or other confidence-guided decoding methods. The only baseline is vanilla CFG (which doubles cost) and direct inference.

Efficiency claims are qualitative: no wall-clock latency or throughput measurements are reported for the extra sequential forward passes over the three auxiliary tokens per high-entropy position, so 'negligible overhead' is not quantified.

Improvements are inconsistent across tasks: several configurations degrade performance (e.g., Qwen3-8B-Reasoning drops on WinoGrande at most thresholds), and the paper does not characterize when the method helps versus hurts.

No code release is mentioned; given the many implementation-specific details (exact KV-cache reuse procedure, injection timing, threshold semantics), released code would substantially strengthen reproducibility.

Presentation issues: grammatical errors, inconsistent prompt naming between Fig. 3c ('STATUS ERROR/TRUE') and the text ('OUTPUT ERROR/TRUE'), and unclear semantics of the τ values in Table 1 reduce clarity.
The word-cloud and single-case-study analyses are anecdotal and provide limited scientific evidence for the claimed mechanisms (increased lexical diversity, abandoning erroneous chains).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical observation: reasoning failures concentrate in a small set of high-entropy tokens (Fig. 1), which directly motivates the intervention and is supported by a follow-up mechanistic analysis (Fig. 4) showing low-entropy tokens are largely 'immune' to CFG modification.

The proposed method is simple, training-free, and practically attractive: selective CFG applied only at high-entropy tokens plus KV-cache reuse with negative-prompt injection, which removes the dual-KV-cache overhead of LLM-CFG and enables plug-and-play deployment with modern inference stacks.

Broad and generally convincing evaluation: five LLMs across scales/families, six benchmarks spanning general, coding, and STEM tasks, a stochastic-sampling check on AIME2024 (8 runs), a VLM extension, latency measurements, and ablations over the entropy threshold, guidance scale, and negative prompt.

Useful analysis sections: comparison against SOTA test-time scaling methods (Table 5), a contrastive-decoding comparison (Table 7), entropy-scope analysis (Table 6) supporting the selectivity claim, and case studies illustrating failure modes.
The paper is generally well written, the method is clearly specified (Equations 1-5), and the OpenCompass configuration setup supports reproducibility of the evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: Per-model hyperparameter selection appears post-hoc: the best threshold tau differs across models and the headline gains correspond to the best cell of a 5-point sweep per model (green cells in Tables 1-2). Without a pre-registered, held-out selection procedure applied uniformly, reported averages may overstate expected gains; the paper acknowledges cross-validation 'can be' used but does not demonstrate it.

Main results use greedy decoding only, and statistical significance/error bars are absent for most benchmarks; single-run results on noisy tasks (e.g., GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench) make some individual deltas hard to interpret. The sampling validation is limited to one benchmark (AIME2024).

Some baselines appear weak or oddly configured: DeepSeek-R1-7B direct inference scores 29.29 on GPQA-D due to degenerate repetition, and Vanilla CFG uses the same negative prompt as MTI; comparisons to stronger decoding baselines in the main table (e.g., entropy-aware methods in Related Work such as entropy-gated branching, DoT) are absent from the main results and relegated to brief qualitative contrasts.

Novelty is moderate: the method is a combination of existing ideas (LLM-CFG from Sanchez et al. 2023, entropy-based token selection from prior work, negative prompting from diffusion models); the contribution is primarily an engineering/empirical one rather than a new principle.

The 'OUTPUT ERROR' negative-prompt mechanism is ad hoc; while the ablation (Fig. 3c, Table 8) is informative, there is no principled explanation of why a two-word cue yields a well-calibrated unconditional branch, and the claimed superior approximation of the unconditional distribution (Fig. 2b) is asserted rather than measured.

A few quantitative claims are imprecise (e.g., '+9.28% average improvement' is actually an absolute point gain, and comparisons like '73.34% vs 73.75%' highlight marginal differences presented as findings); some ablation conclusions (negative-prompt ranking) rest on small differences without variance estimates.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across five LLMs (Qwen3 family, DeepSeek-R1-7B, Ling-mini-2.0), three task domains (general, coding, STEM), and a VLM extension, which is broader coverage than typical decoding-strategy papers

The core observation (reasoning errors concentrated in a small fraction of high-entropy tokens) is clearly motivated and supported by Fig. 1 and the Fig. 4 analysis of where CFG actually changes predictions

The KV-cache reuse with negative-prompt injection is a practical engineering contribution that removes the dual-cache overhead of LLM-CFG, with a latency analysis (Table 3) showing the intervention can even reduce wall-clock time

Multiple ablations (entropy threshold, guidance scale ω, negative prompt choice), comparison to contrastive decoding (Appendix A.3), comparison to several test-time scaling methods (Table 5), and stochastic-decoding validation with 8 runs on AIME2024
The paper is generally well organized and the plug-and-play nature of the method makes it easy for practitioners to adopt
weaknesses: Limited novelty: both ingredients exist in prior work the paper itself cites — LLM-CFG (Sanchez et al., 2023), entropy-gated/entropy-based token selection (Li et al., 2025b; Qian et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). The contribution is essentially a combination (selective application + KV-cache reuse), and the paper does not clearly delineate what is new relative to entropy-gated branching in particular

The central causal claim is under-justified. Figure 1 shows incorrect answers have higher entropy, but this is correlational: high entropy may be a consequence of being on a wrong reasoning path rather than the cause of error propagation. No analysis disentangles the two (e.g., perturbing high-entropy tokens on correct trajectories)

The claim that reusing the conditional KV cache and appending 'OUTPUT ERROR' yields a 'superior approximation of the unconditional distribution' (Fig. 2 caption) is asserted but never substantiated. Injecting a negative-prompt suffix into the conditional context defines an arbitrary contrast distribution, not the unconditional one; the theoretical framing of Sec. 3.3 is loose

Statistical rigor is thin: most results use greedy decoding with no variance estimates or significance tests, and several benchmarks are small (GPQA-Diamond ~198 items, AIME2024 30 items), so gains of 1–2 points are hard to distinguish from noise. Only AIME2024 uses 8 sampling runs

Hyperparameter sensitivity undermines the 'robust green zone' claim: Table 1 shows configurations that substantially underperform direct inference (e.g., Ling-mini-2.0 with τ=2.0 drops ~9 points below DI; DeepSeek-R1-7B τ=2.0 underperforms DI on MATH500/HEval). Optimal τ varies by model and dataset, and the paper concedes it must be tuned via cross-validation on a held-out set

Some comparisons are questionable in framing: Table 5 compares against efficiency-oriented methods (TALE, NoThinking, DEER, CGRS) whose goal is reducing token budgets, whereas MTI does not reduce computation in the same sense, so 'superiority' over these baselines conflates different objectives

Qualitative analyses (word-cloud 'lexical diversity' claims in Sec. 4.4, the case study in Fig. 6) are anecdotal and interpretively stretched; the claimed mechanism (MTI 'initiates new lines of thought' via connectives) is speculation, not evidence

Reproducibility concerns: the code link appears truncated/incomplete ('The code can be found'), only OpenCompass config filenames are listed, and details such as how the negative prompt is tokenized/positioned relative to the cache are not fully specified

Presentation issues: Fig. 1 inset labels are garbled, Figs. 3a/3c are hard to read, and there are noticeable typos (e.g., 'Fig. 2b proposes a selective...', 'We use LLMs to polish my papers'), suggesting insufficient proofreading

strengths: Practical, training-free decoding method: applying classifier-free guidance only at high-entropy tokens is simple, plug-and-play, and well-motivated by the empirical observation (Fig. 1, Fig. 4) that CFG-induced top-1 changes concentrate in high-entropy positions.

Broad empirical coverage: five models across scales (Qwen3-8B/14B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-7B, Ling-mini-2.0), six benchmarks spanning general, coding, and STEM tasks, plus an extension to vision-language models, which strengthens the generality claim beyond a single setting.

Reasonable ablation suite: entropy threshold (τ), guidance strength (ω), negative prompt choice (including negative vs. positive vs. meaningless prompts), comparison with contrastive decoding under the MTI framework, and a latency analysis (Table 3) that goes beyond FLOP counts.

The KV-cache reuse trick for the unconditional branch is an engineering contribution of independent interest, addressing a real practical obstacle (dual KV caches) for deploying CFG-style decoding with vLLM-style serving stacks.

Comparison against several recent test-time scaling baselines (TALE, NoThinking, Dynasor, DEER, CGRS) in Appendix A.2, and evaluation under both greedy and stochastic decoding adds some robustness evidence.
Adequate reproducibility signals: OpenCompass configuration files listed, decoding hyperparameters specified, code release promised.
weaknesses: The central 'unconditional branch' claim is conceptually shaky. Appending 'OUTPUT ERROR' to the conditional context is not an unconditional distribution in any principled sense; Eq. (1)'s CFG formulation does not cleanly apply, and the paper offers no theoretical or empirical validation that this branch approximates the unconditional distribution. The method may work simply as an adversarial perturbation, which is a different mechanism than claimed.

The motivating analysis (Fig. 1) is purely correlational. High answer entropy correlates with errors, but there is no causal control—for example, applying the same intervention at a matched number of randomly selected tokens—to establish that high-entropy positions specifically are where intervention helps.

Baseline anomalies raise fairness concerns. The DI score of 29.29% on GPQA-Diamond for DeepSeek-R1-7B (vs. 51.52% with MTI) points to degenerate repetition under greedy decoding, so headline gains partly reflect fixing a broken baseline. Gains under sampling (AIME2024, Table 2) are more modest (+4–5%). It is unclear whether SOTA baselines in Table 5 (e.g., NoThinking at 30.0 for Qwen3-8B) were implemented and tuned comparably.

Statistical rigor is thin for Table 1: single greedy runs with no variance or significance testing; Table 2 reports means over 8 runs but no standard deviations or significance tests, despite the AIME sample size (30 problems) making fluctuations large.

The 'negligible overhead' claim is overstated: CFG usage reaches 30–50% of tokens at small τ, and Table 3 shows latency can be substantially worse than DI (e.g., Qwen-14B at τ=0.1: 6081s vs. 4547s). The efficiency story depends heavily on choosing larger τ, at which point gains shrink.

The 'OUTPUT ERROR' cue is an ad-hoc magic string; while the negative-prompt ablation is interesting, the robustness of the overall method appears tied to this heuristic, and per-dataset/per-model threshold selection (τ) reintroduces tuning burden the framing tries to deny.

Presentation and rigor issues: duplicated sentence in Related Works; abstract's truncated code link; duplicated identical Guo et al. 2025a/b references; typos ('excessively τ', 'which can induce reasoning even for low-entropy tokens' in the case study); the word-cloud analysis (Fig. 5) is anecdotal and its interpretation is post-hoc.
Writing quality and polish issues, plus an odd LLM-use disclosure, slightly undermine confidence in overall manuscript care.
